episode.title: Beware of These Five Fallacies!
episode.tagline: Our brains are hardwired to think in ways suited to a pre-historic world -- which is why there are so many fallacies in our thinking!
episode.about: In this episode, Amit and Ajay discuss five foundational fallacies, and speak about how we can improve our thinking if we learn to recognise them and avoid them.

items.topic: Ryan, the push-ups, and a deliberate post-hoc fallacy
items.summary: In the late 1980s and early 1990s at Ferguson College, Pune, Amit was so thin you could count his ribs. Fresh from a boys' school and in an arts class that was about 80% girls, he chose between the canteen and the tapri based on the wind, so his shirt would not blow against his ribs. Gyms were not yet part of the culture. His consolation was Ryan, a devout Christian who was just as thin. Then one day, through Ryan's open hostel door, Amit saw him doing push-ups. Ryan explained that masturbation was a sin, and he had set himself 25 push-ups as the penance for each time. Six months later Ryan was buff, a 'Greek god', and Amit was the only one left with visible ribs. When another hostel friend (Amit gives him a pseudonym, Varun) quietly asked how to get a body like Ryan's, Amit told him, deliberately and as a joke: you have to masturbate.
items.insight: This is post hoc ergo propter hoc in its purest form. One thing happened, then another, so the first must have caused the second. The joke works because the real cause, the push-ups, was hidden inside the sequence. Many of our causal stories leave out the hidden middle step in the same way.
items.quote: The lesson here is that deliberately out of a sense of humor, I committed a fallacy called the post hoc ergo propter hoc.

items.topic: The witch doctor's coat and the flooding Nile
items.summary: A witch doctor claims that every spring he takes off his coat, and then the Nile floods, so the river must be responding to his coat. The sequence is real: spring, then coat, then flood. The causal claim is absurd. Ajay adds a thought experiment. If pressing a button gives you a biscuit one second later, two or three tries convince you that you caused it. Stretch the delay to 10 seconds and it gets harder. At 10 hours the mind can no longer connect the two.
items.insight: Our sense of causality was built for a simple world of tigers and deer, where effects follow causes quickly. Today's information environment is far more complex, and many important processes play out over long timescales. So we have to lean on evidence and data rather than gut feel.
items.quote: The witch doctor would claim that in spring, I take off my coat, and then the Nile floods. So the Nile responds to my action on the coat.

items.topic: The coin in the crowded swimming pool
items.summary: Amit recalls a metaphor from his friend Shruti Rajagopalan, who he thinks may have been quoting Don Boudreaux. Does dropping a coin into water raise the water level? In a lab, with a beaker and everything controlled, the answer is easy. Now try it in a huge, crowded swimming pool where people are splashing, it is windy and it is raining. The data will mostly be garbage. Amit says this is why economists love the post-war splits of North and South Korea and East and West Germany. They come close to a controlled experiment on free markets, and 'spoiler alert, free markets won'.
items.insight: Social science happens in the swimming pool, not the beaker. Real controlled experiments are rare, and confirmation bias fills the gap. So claims that X caused Y deserve humility and caution.
items.quote: Now imagine you are doing this in a crowded swimming pool. It's a big swimming pool, it is incredibly crowded, people are splashing around in it, it is windy and it is raining at the same time.

items.topic: What really caused the Great Depression?
items.summary: The standard story is that the 1929 stock market crash caused the Great Depression. Drawing on Thomas Sowell, Amit points out that unemployment in the months after the crash peaked at about 9% and was down to around 6.5% by June 1930. Then the government began to intervene, starting with the Smoot-Hawley tariff and followed by a series of other interventions, and things exploded. Sowell also notes a later stock market crash that was followed by decades of strong growth. Amit adds that he thinks Amity Shlaes has a book making a similar case.
items.insight: A dramatic event followed by a disaster makes an easy causal story. The less visible chain of policy decisions in between can matter far more. Blaming the obvious trigger is a post-hoc fallacy at the scale of history.
items.quote: It wasn't the stock market crash. It was a whole bunch of interventions which led to the problem.

items.topic: The tomato glut and the coming chip glut
items.summary: When tomatoes are scarce, a farmer reasons that he should plant tomatoes, spend heavily on inputs and make a killing. That is sensible for one farmer. But a million farmers respond to the same prices, the market floods, prices collapse to zero, and angry farmers dump truckloads of tomatoes on the roadside because transporting them isn't worth it. Ajay sees the same pattern with semiconductors: after the chip shortage, 'every idiot in the world' decided to build a fab. He predicts a glut and bankruptcies among chipmakers within a year or two.
items.insight: This is the fallacy of composition in action. What is rational for one actor can be ruinous when everyone does it. The disciplined question is always: what happens if everybody does this?
items.quote: What may be true for me in the small doesn't work when a million people think the same.

items.topic: The dart-throwing monkey and the Infosys IPO
items.summary: In finance it is well accepted that a monkey throwing darts builds a decent portfolio, and that nearly all clever humans picking stocks underperform it. Yet each of us thinks we are in the elite 0.01%. Ajay extends this to careers. Nobody could have predicted the software boom from the mid-90s, and the Infosys IPO was mostly undersubscribed. Insiders in a booming industry then credit their success to their own decisions. The honest test is to ask how you would have done if you had simply bought shares in 10 companies in your industry and done nothing. Only the outperformance over that baseline is yours.
items.insight: Much of 'success' comes from the luck of being in software rather than seafood. Separate the industry tailwind from your own contribution before crediting the CEO, or yourself.
items.quote: The world, the society attributes all firm success to the CEO, and I think that is wrong.

items.item: Economic Facts and Fallacies
items.creator: Thomas Sowell
items.context: The framework for the whole episode. Its opening chapters lay out the five foundational fallacies the hosts discuss.
items.reason: Sowell is one of Amit's intellectual heroes, 'still going strong at ninety plus'. The book names fallacies that are foundational, in that many other errors grow out of them. Understanding these frailties makes our thinking clearer.

items.item: The Double 'Thank You' Moment
items.creator: John Stossel
items.context: Used to rebut the zero-sum fallacy. Stossel is 'one of my favorite columnists ever'.
items.reason: When you buy coffee, both you and the seller say thank you because both are better off. It is the simplest illustration that voluntary exchange is positive-sum.

items.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10 of Everything is Everything)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.context: Cited for its chart of world GDP, flat for centuries and then shooting up.
items.reason: It shows that as industrialisation, travel and free markets multiplied double thank-you moments, value and innovation exploded. This is the economic history behind the positive-sum world.

items.item: Profit = Philanthropy
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.context: The column behind Amit's line that the pursuit of profit is the greatest form of philanthropy.
items.reason: In a world of voluntary exchange, the only way to profit is by making someone else better off. Profit is therefore an incentive to do good for others.

items.item: The Great Redistribution
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.context: The column Amit links when he jokingly names a law of economics after himself.
items.reason: It uses tariffs to show that interfering with free markets usually redistributes wealth from poor consumers to the narrow interest groups that lobbied for the interference.

items.item: The Evolution of Cooperation
items.creator: Robert Axelrod
items.context: Raised after Amit argued for generosity over crabby, zero-sum behaviour in personal life.
items.reason: Ajay calls it 'a fabulous book'. It formalises the optimal response to being wronged: strike back once, but not twice, not thrice, not forever. Some punishment is optimal, grudges are not. That is very different from the behaviour of warlike tribes.

items.item: Tim Urban's tweet on getting to know people
items.creator: Tim Urban
items.context: Read out while discussing the danger of judging individuals by their group, or by one opinion.
items.reason: 'Whenever I get to know someone who seems perfect, I end up disappointed. Whenever I get to know someone who I think is the worst of the worst, I'm pleasantly surprised. Angels and demons aren't real.' It is a reminder to judge people less and stay open to them.

items.item: The Day Ryan Started Masturbating
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.context: Linked in the show notes as the written version of the college story Amit tells to explain the post-hoc fallacy.
items.reason: It is the full telling of the episode's funniest illustration of mistaking sequence for causation.

items.item: 'Wet streets cause rain' (Michael Crichton on Gell-Mann Amnesia)
items.creator: Michael Crichton
items.context: Amit borrows Crichton's phrase for getting causation backwards.
items.reason: It is a memorable label for reverse causation: you see wet streets and rain together and conclude the streets caused the rain.

items.item: The Forgotten Man
items.creator: Amity Shlaes
items.context: Mentioned ('if I remember correctly') as also arguing that the 1929 crash alone did not cause the Great Depression.
items.reason: It supports Sowell's case that government interventions, not the stock market crash, turned a downturn into a depression.

items.item: Poker and Life (Episode 38 of Everything is Everything)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.context: Recalled while drawing the personal lesson from the post-hoc fallacy.
items.reason: Most of what happens to us is sheer dumb luck. Don't let success go to your head or failure crush you, and focus on doing the right things.

items.item: The Man of System (excerpted from The Theory of Moral Sentiments)
items.creator: Adam Smith
items.context: Amit calls it a 'brilliant passage' and the origin of the chess-pieces fallacy.
items.reason: It is the classic statement of the arrogance of imagining society as pieces on a chessboard that a planner can move at will.

items.item: The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism
items.creator: Friedrich Hayek
items.context: Cited as Hayek's name for the chess-pieces fallacy.
items.reason: Hayek's 'fatal conceit' is the belief that we can control a complex world from the top down. Beyond a certain level of complexity, no one has the information to do so.

items.item: The Use of Knowledge in Society
items.creator: Friedrich Hayek
items.context: Referred to as 'Hayek's great essay' while explaining spontaneous order.
items.reason: It is the foundation for understanding why order can emerge without a top-down plan, and why central planners can never gather all the knowledge they need.

items.item: Four Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41 of Everything is Everything)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.context: 'An episode I really love', where the hosts discussed Hayek's essay and spontaneous order.
items.reason: A deeper dive into the ideas behind the chess-pieces fallacy.

items.item: What's Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18 of Everything is Everything)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.context: Mentioned by Ajay while giving the tomato-glut example of the fallacy of composition.
items.reason: The earlier episode covered how farmers chasing the same high prices produce gluts and collapsing prices.

items.item: The Selfish Gene
items.creator: Richard Dawkins
items.context: Ajay says the chess-pieces fallacy 'goes all the way to selfish gene'.
items.reason: Every organism optimises for itself, so you can never suppress each person's drive to pursue their own life, liberty and happiness. That is why top-down control keeps failing.

items.item: Untitled
items.creator: Leonard Cohen
items.context: 'I can't resist recommending' it. Ajay used it as an epigraph at the end of the technology-policy chapter of his book with Vijay Kelkar.
items.reason: It is a slave speaking, saying that any system you design without us will not work. A poetic version of why top-down designs fail.

items.item: In Service of the Republic
items.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
items.context: Mentioned as 'the Kelkar and Shah book', where the Leonard Cohen poem serves as an epigraph to the technology-policy chapter.
items.reason: It is Ajay's own treatment of economic policy, in which the limits of top-down system design are a recurring theme.

items.item: Understanding the State (Episode 25 of Everything is Everything)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.context: Recalled during the open-ended fallacy: 'we have done an episode in the past' on how every act of government is an act of violence.
items.reason: The state acts through coercion, starting with taxation. That makes every government rupee carry an opportunity cost.

items.item: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26 of Everything is Everything)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.context: Ajay points to 'our pair of episodes' on when the state should act and what it should do.
items.reason: It brings two big ideas to policy: the no-free-lunch budget constraint, and the fact that coercive power has no such constraint.

items.item: The Economics and Politics of Vaccines (Episode 223 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Ajay Shah)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.context: Linked when Ajay argued that Indian health policy should shift from healthcare to public health.
items.reason: Ajay explains in detail there why prevention beats cure, and why the distinction between public health and healthcare matters.

items.item: Declutter (Episode 30 of Everything is Everything)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.context: Amit thinks they discussed the personal side of the open-ended fallacy there.
items.reason: It covers recognising the constraints in our own lives, especially time, and prioritising accordingly.

items.item: Why We Fight: The Roots of War and the Paths to Peace
items.creator: Christopher Blattman
items.context: Ajay's recommendation for the week, prompted by Amit opening the episode by asking why we fight.
items.reason: Ajay is glad an economist has 'opened the box of violence'. Taming violence, both between citizens and between state and citizens, is central to the development story, and economists usually stick to money and markets.

items.item: The Three Languages of Politics
items.creator: Arnold Kling
items.context: Amit's recommendation for the week, on the theme of why we fight.
items.reason: It is a slim book you can read in an hour. Kling shows that ideological tribes talk past each other because they start from different core values: equality for left-liberals, tradition for conservatives, freedom for libertarians. Recognising the other side's value is the way to find common ground.

items.item: In My Tribe
items.creator: Arnold Kling
items.context: Mentioned alongside the book. Kling 'used to be a great blogger' and now has a newsletter 'you must subscribe to'.
items.reason: It continues Kling's thinking, and Amit recalls a follow-up there or elsewhere that adds nuance to the three-languages framework.

items.item: The Populist Playbook (Episode 42 of Everything is Everything)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.context: Ajay connects Kling's framework to the 'wolves and sheep' theme of that episode.
items.reason: The sheep come in three flocks with different values, but all of them share an overarching interest in not being trampled by the wolves.

items.concept: Stone Age brains in a modern world
items.explanation: The world is too complex to grasp, so we make sense of it through simple stories. Those stories clash with each other, and sometimes all of them clash with reality. Our instincts were forged for small hunter-gatherer tribes. Ajay adds that the roughly 4,000 generations of modern humans are too few to change that 'hardware'. Many fallacies are instincts that once worked and now misfire.
items.quote: From a hundred thousand years ago to today, the period of modern man is a mere 4,000 generations, which is not enough to materially move the needle on our hardware.

items.concept: Why we disagree: facts, values and the reasoning engine
items.explanation: Ajay's triad. We reason from facts (skewed by overweighting personal experience), from values (partly our birthright, often muddled), and through a reasoning engine. Disagreement comes from a difference in one of the three. The hope is that the reasoning engine, meaning logic, argument and proof, can be common ground for a shared notion of truth.
items.quote: Maybe there are certain universal stories of logic, of argument, of proof, which we can all agree on, and we can construct a social shared notion of truth.

items.explanation: When a tribe splits a deer, every chunk I take is one you can't have. Modern exchange is different: voluntary transactions leave both sides better off. Zero-sum thinking drives statism and the confusion of inequality with poverty. Since 1991, hundreds of millions of Indians have left poverty even as inequality rose. Treating the economy as a fixed pie favours redistribution over growth and wrecks incentives. On a personal level, Amit argues against crabby scarcity thinking and for generosity, because someone else's success is not your loss.
items.quote: In a world of double thank you moments, the only way that I can profit is by making you better off.

items.concept: Knowledge is the greatest positive-sum game
items.explanation: Ajay's extension of the zero-sum argument. Newton, the Magna Carta and the transistor were created in some corner, and everyone got better off. The inventors of the transistor did not gain at our expense. Accumulated human knowledge is a public good whose spillovers transform everything.
items.quote: The emergence of culture and the development of knowledge is just a public good and it spills over, it inflects everything, and it is the greatest positive sum game story of the world.

items.concept: Intervention redistributes from the poor to the rich
items.explanation: Amit's self-named 'law'. Interfering with free markets usually transfers wealth upward. With tariffs, competition shrinks and ordinary consumers pay more or get less. The value they lose goes to the narrow interest groups that lobbied for the tariff.
items.quote: Most interference in free markets leads to a redistribution from the poor to the rich.

items.explanation: This is the belief that what is true of a part is true of the whole. Politicians help one group and present its gains as gains for society, which is really robbing Peter to pay Paul. Ajay sees it as the core difference between thinking like a firm and thinking about an economy. Exporting more makes sense for one company, but using state power to subsidise land, electricity or the exchange rate so that every company exports can unbalance the economy. The test to always apply is: what if everyone does it?
items.quote: A baseball fan at a ballpark can see the game better by standing up. But if all the fans stand up, they will not all see better.

items.concept: The flip side: don't judge individuals by their group
items.explanation: Amit inverts the fallacy of composition. Stereotyping takes a trait attributed to a group, or seen in one member, and paints every individual with it. One sociopathic economist doesn't make all economists sociopaths. The same applies to condemning someone as evil over a single disagreement on social media. People regress to the mean: neither angels nor demons.
items.quote: We are all human, we are all frail, and we are all beautiful.

items.concept: A country is not a company
items.explanation: Ajay previews a future episode. Successful businesspeople assume their skills carry over to government, but they mostly don't, for two reasons. First, economy-wide actions trigger composition effects that a single firm never faces. Second, government wields coercive power, which firms largely lack.
items.quote: In a firm, you don't have much coercive power. Whereas when you're a government, you are dealing with the poison every day of coercive power.

items.concept: The post-hoc fallacy and its cousins
items.explanation: The post-hoc fallacy assumes that because B followed A, A caused B. Its cousin, cum hoc ergo propter hoc, assumes that two simultaneous events must be causally linked. Michael Crichton's 'wet streets cause rain' gets the arrow backwards. These made sense in a simple world where a rustle in the bush meant a tiger. Amit argues that religion and ritual grew from such simple causal stories, for example about what causes rain. In a complex world they mislead us constantly, especially in economics.
items.quote: Something happened, something happened after it. Therefore the first thing caused the second thing.

items.concept: Our causal radar has a short range
items.explanation: If the biscuit arrives one second after the button press, we see causality instantly. If it arrives 10 hours later, we are lost. Many processes in the universe play out over long timescales, exactly where our intuition fails. So we must push harder to be evidence-based before making causal claims.
items.quote: The human mind is congenitally unable to see cause and effect playing out across longer timescales.

items.concept: Luck dominates, so judge yourself against the baseline
items.explanation: Amit's personal lesson: most of what happens to us is luck. Don't build stories like 'I am good, so good things happened' or 'I am bad, so bad things happened'. Keep doing the right thing, your dharma. Ajay's version for firms is to compare your results with simply holding your industry's stocks. Only the outperformance is your contribution.
items.quote: 98% of what happens to each of us is sheer dumb luck.

items.explanation: Adam Smith's 'man of system' and Hayek's 'fatal conceit' describe the belief that society is a static chessboard a planner can arrange. Top-down control works for a tribe or a 10-person family firm. At scale, no one has the information, and spontaneous order emerges from 'human action, but not human design'. Amit says millions of Indians stayed poor longer than they should have because planners did not trust people's ingenuity. Ajay is less sure the lesson has been learned. For individuals, the lesson is to focus on processes and habits, not grand goals.
items.quote: The truth is we are not pieces on a chessboard that you can make things go the way they want.

items.concept: The open-ended fallacy and no free lunch
items.explanation: Health, safety and open space are open-ended desires, but resources are limited and have alternative uses. Amit says India's biggest religion is government: we assume 'mai-baap sarkar' will pay for everything, as if money were unlimited and costless. Yet every government rupee is extracted through taxation, which is coercive and costly, so it has an opportunity cost. Ajay invokes Milton Friedman's 'no free lunch'. A responsible policy thinker should pair every proposal for more spending with matching cuts elsewhere.
items.quote: Many desirable things are advocated without regard to the most fundamental fact of economics, that resources are inherently limited and have alternative uses.

items.concept: The sophisticated health expert asks for less government healthcare spending
items.explanation: Ajay offers a contrarian test of expertise. The Indian government spends poorly, and prevention is better than cure. So the right plea is to reorient the system away from healthcare and towards public health, meaning preventive measures, rather than to demand more money for the same things.
items.quote: I consider it a hallmark of health expertise in India that the plea of a sophisticated health expert in India should be to cut down government spending on health care.

items.explanation: Spending is at least capped by what the state can raise. Coercion has no such cap. A government can ban one thing after another and whittle away freedoms day by day with nothing to stop it. So actions that reduce freedom deserve even more scrutiny than actions that cost money.
items.quote: In spending, there is a budget constraint. It adds up to 100, and you don't have more than 100 rupees to spend. But unfortunately, when it gets to coercion, coercion can be limitless.

items.concept: Your time is the open-ended fallacy you live with
items.explanation: Amit's personal version. With age, the binding constraint shifts from money to time. We act under an illusion of immortality and try to give our minds to everything. He cites Steve Jobs's advice to his designer Jonathan Ive: pick a couple of things, say no to the rest, even the ones you love. This is not about a productivity fetish, since time to relax and chill out is useful too.
items.quote: Learn to say no to things that you love.

items.explanation: Arnold Kling argues that political tribes talk past each other because their core values differ: equality for left-liberals, tradition for conservatives, freedom for libertarians and classical liberals. Arguing in your own value's language is pointless. Amit gives an example: with a left-winger, he argues that a statist intervention hurts the poor rather than that it reduces freedom. Ajay adds that the sheep come in three flocks, but all share an interest in not being trampled by the wolves.
items.quote: One way to get past the fighting that we do, this ideological bickering that has become so common, is to recognize the other person's core first principle, which is also to recognize that other person's humanity.

items.explanation: Ajay's closing plea. Knowing these fallacies is easy, but internalising them takes a long time. Exam-driven, credential-focused India has a sterile idea of knowledge as a trade you apply, and real reasoning has been pushed out of most people's consciousness. Thinking about thinking is a skill, and it can be learned.
items.quote: In modern doctor, engineer, MBA, accountant, lawyer India, there is a great crisis of thinking.

items.content: The episode opens with both hosts fumbling over who should speak first. Amit turns it into the thesis: 'both of us wanted the other one to go first, and we ended up kind of fighting over it. Not really a fight, but it's a good question. Why do we keep fighting?'
Amit scripts his own cue and Ajay obliges. Amit: 'How does your first fallacy involve hunting? I love it how you follow my instructions and ask me all the questions I want.'

On catching Ryan doing push-ups: 'this goes against the ethical code... thin boys whose bones are visible don't do push-ups.' After hearing the penance explanation: 'in my mind, I did sashtang pranam and I just left.'
Six months later the girls are 'giggling at the improbable presence of a Greek god in their midst... and now I am the only person whose bones are visible.'
Explaining cum hoc ergo propter hoc, Amit admits: 'I love the name because of the main activity in the story.'

On Ajay's biscuit experiment: 'I'm on keto diet, so if I press a button, I don't want a biscuit to come ever. Bacon strips, another matter.' He later reveals his keto plus one-meal-a-day plan: 'because I want to be like Ryan. Which Ryan do I want to be like? Any of the two.'

Amit, on not generalising about economists: 'we know many economists who are sociopaths, Ajay, I want to tell you that, but I know you're not one of them. You're a deeply emotional and empathetic person.'
Amit points to a graph and then corrects himself: 'when I say as you can see, I mean you, gentle reader. He can't see any graph on the screen. There's no screen, there's only me.'
Amit, unabashed: 'I'm gonna be a little vain. I'm gonna name a law of economics after myself because I keep talking about it and no one seems to get it.'

Ajay on investor hubris: the dart-throwing monkey beats nearly all stock pickers, 'Of course, hope springs eternal. We each of us think that I'm in that 0.01% of the cool people that know what to do.'
Ajay teases Amit's claim that India has learned to distrust top-down planning: 'Gentle readers, see how optimistic Amit is.'
In an episode about why we fight, Ajay says Amit opened by 'whining'. Amit: 'I wasn't whining and we will fight over the use of your word whining. I don't whine.'
'PPP: perpetually planned poverty', a phrase coined by the hosts' mutual friend Kumar Anand for what statism and zero-sum thinking produce.
'Mai-baap sarkar kar degi' (the parent-government will provide). Amit says India's 'biggest religion is government', the mindset that powers the open-ended fallacy.
Adam Ferguson's phrase that things happen through 'human action, but not human design', invoked with Hayek to describe spontaneous order.
Milton Friedman's 'no free lunch', Ajay's shorthand for the fact that government money is neither free nor infinite.
Robert Trivers's work on altruism and self-interest, cited by Amit to argue that we are hardwired for both, and that being altruistic indirectly serves our self-interest.

'Pessimism of the intellect, optimism of the will', the phrase Amit uses to answer the gloom: we see what is wrong but keep fighting. He followed it with 'Everything is everything' and then admitted it 'was a dramatic way to end the chapter'.

threads.name: Thinking like an economist: prices, incentives and the unseen
threads.summary: Why do well-meant policies so often hurt the people they aim to help? This thread builds the hosts' core toolkit: the seen and the unseen, prices as carriers of information, and the fallacies our Stone Age brains fall for. It then puts the tools to work on farms, power grids, the rupee and gig work.

path.why: The two foundations: Bastiat's seen and unseen, and Hayek's insight that prices coordinate what no planner could know.
Friedman, Hayek, Coase and Bastiat: three papers and an essay that teach frames, not just conclusions.
Hazlitt's one lesson, trace the longer effects on all groups, applied to public works, taxes, tariffs and rent control.
Zero-sum, composition, post hoc, chess pieces, open-ended: five traps our Stone Age brains fall into.
Price caps, rent control, minimum wages, MSPs and tariffs: what happens every time the state fiddles with prices.
Beliefs that make elites feel virtuous while hurting the poor, from socialism and inequality to banning victimless crimes.
The toolkit on a real crisis: storage isn't hoarding, speculation is insurance, and APMC monopsonies squeeze farmers.
Prices to the rescue: flexible electricity prices bridge the gap between solar power at noon and demand at dusk.
The most important price of all, and why calling the rupee 'strong' or 'weak' is meaningless.
Steelmans the critics, then asks 'better than what?' to argue gig work means freedom and empowerment.
The capstone: the ten frameworks that shaped the hosts, from spontaneous order to the double thank-you moment.

bigIdeas.name: The double thank-you moment: the world is positive-sum
bigIdeas.summary: When you buy coffee, you value the coffee more than the money and the seller values the money more than the coffee, so both say thank you. Every voluntary exchange leaves both sides better off, so more exchange means more wealth; our zero-sum instincts, formed splitting a deer within a tribe, miss this, and the growth of knowledge is the greatest positive-sum game of all. Markets are not a third pillar set against society but a web of double thank-you moments, in which the only way to profit is to make someone else better off. War is the negative-sum alternative, and when trade breaks down, nations start thinking about seizing what they can no longer buy.
bigIdeas.why: It separates capitalism, which is consent, from cronyism, and it is why the hosts treat freedom and trade as humanitarian questions rather than abstractions. Every voluntary trade that is blocked destroys value that would otherwise have existed.

bigIdeas.name: Stone-age hardware, cultural software
bigIdeas.summary: Our instincts were tuned for small hunter-gatherer bands, and some 4,000 generations of modern humans are too few to change that hardware: we crave sugar, see danger in outsiders, think in zero-sum and top-down terms and want a strongman for the tribe. Culture is the operating system on top, and only humans can examine and rewrite it; nature gives you knobs, nurture turns them. That is why prices, spontaneous order and liberty feel unintuitive and have to be won again by every generation, and why describing our wiring never justifies it: you do not get to an ought from an is.
bigIdeas.why: It explains why bad economics and strongmen stay perennially popular, and it offers a personal tool: notice when an instinct built for a charging lion is firing at a rude email from your boss, and let culture and reason dampen it.

bigIdeas.name: Index every belief on a zero-to-one scale
bigIdeas.summary: Ajay tags everything he believes on a zero-to-one scale of how sure he is and whether it came from authority or his own reasoning, and argues that calibrating uncertainty, not 'everyone has their own truth', is the real skill. Good thinkers update in proportion to the quality of the evidence: shifting your view by 10% after a strong argument is gold and saying 'I was wrong' is the summit, while the traps are deference to famous names and the arrogance of conclusions you worked hard to reach. Amit's version is to be open on facts but firm on values, and both hosts urge being sceptical of tradition and convention, and analytical rather than reverential about great figures, without being dismissive.
bigIdeas.why: It protects against both post-truth relativism and smug certainty, and gives a test for experts: a complex world allows only answers like '70% this, 20% that', so beware anyone incentivised to exude certainty.

bigIdeas.name: The seen and the unseen
bigIdeas.summary: Bastiat's broken window: the glazier's earnings are seen, while the coat or book the owner would otherwise have bought is unseen. Hazlitt's one lesson generalises it: the bad economist looks at the immediate effect on one visible group, the good one traces the longer effects on everyone. State spending raises GDP even when it creates nothing, and each rupee of it costs the economy about three; a tariff hides the consumers who pay and the protected firm that stops improving; a cautious drug regulator hides the lives lost to delay. Good intentions are seen and bad consequences unseen, so compassion has to be judged by outcomes.
bigIdeas.why: It is the first question to ask of any policy, subsidy or 'stimulus': what would that money and those people have done otherwise, and who bears the costs nobody sees? It works on yourself too: the dopamine of 'one game' of Candy Crush is seen, the less-informed future self is not.

bigIdeas.name: The knowledge problem: no planner can know what prices know
bigIdeas.summary: Knowledge about wants and circumstances is scattered across millions of people, changes constantly and is often unknown even to its holders, so no planner can gather it. Prices solve this: a price is a signal wrapped in an incentive, telling strangers to economise or to produce more without anyone needing to talk. The planner's dream, Adam Smith's 'man of system' or Hayek's 'fatal conceit', treats society as a chessboard whose pieces have no motion of their own, and it keeps coming back, with computers and AI or with regulators who prescribe products and processes.
bigIdeas.why: It explains why central planning brings stagnation, and why India lost much of its post-1991 dynamism once regulators took over the planner's job. Whenever officials propose to decide products, prices or processes, ask who could possibly hold the information to do it well.

Freedom is therefore indivisible: the right objects to what you do in the bedroom and the left to what you do in the marketplace, but consenting adults who harm no one should be left alone in both, whether they trade across the street or across an ocean. Liberalism takes the individual, who contains multitudes, as its unit; ideologies that sort people into groups, from nationalism to wokeism, essentialise and dehumanise, and averages are not identities.
bigIdeas.why: It gives one consistent test that cuts across left and right: is anyone's right being infringed without consent? It also explains the hosts' wariness of 'positive rights' such as a right to food, which require taking from someone else.

bigIdeas.name: Judge the decision, not the outcome
bigIdeas.summary: Because the world is probabilistic, a good decision can turn out badly: a bet that pays 51 paise on heads and costs 49 on tails is worth taking even though you lose half the flips. Poker teaches players to judge their process rather than short-term results and to accept how much is luck, which Amit puts at 98 or 99 percent of what happens to us. Hindsight hides this by turning the probabilistic into the inevitable, so bubbles look obvious, wartime choices look foolish and events look planned, while the law of truly large numbers guarantees that unlikely things happen to someone.
bigIdeas.why: It applies to policies as much as to poker hands, and it makes for a calmer life: less pride in success, less self-blame for good bets that went wrong, and attention on the part you control.

bigIdeas.name: Every act of government is an act of violence
bigIdeas.summary: The state is funded by taxes that nobody would pay unless forced, so whatever it does, it does through violence. That does not make it illegitimate; it is the great liberal paradox: for our rights to mean anything we must give some of them up to a state with a monopoly on violence. So every proposal that 'the state should do X' is a proposal to use coercion and owes a justification, and Amit's diagnostic for any social problem is 'where is the coercion?'. Ajay adds that coercion has no budget constraint: spending is capped by what can be taxed, but rules and bans can be piled on year after year with no ledger.
bigIdeas.why: It reframes every political philosophy as an argument about when this violence is justified. Because coercion is the poison, a good solution does the job with the least of it, and actions that restrict freedom deserve even more scrutiny than ones that merely cost money.

bigIdeas.name: Tribes over principles
bigIdeas.summary: Many people hold principles only because their tribe does and switch when the tribe switches, as many conservatives did when Trump remade the Republican Party; tribes adopt whole packages of dogma, like the green movement's fusion of nuclear power with nuclear bombs, and defend the package even as facts change. Accepting a tribe's entire package is the surest sign someone is not thinking independently, and if a long-argued question looks obvious to you, you have probably shrunk it to a tribal script. The way across is Arnold Kling's insight that progressives, conservatives and libertarians argue in different languages, equality, tradition and freedom, plus steelmanning: stating your opponent's case so well they could have said it themselves.
bigIdeas.why: Caring about being correct, rather than being on the right side, is what makes real updating possible. It is also the hosts' rule for consuming opinion: be suspicious of anyone who toes a whole tribal line.

bigIdeas.summary: Amit's self-named law: every interference in free markets redistributes wealth from the poor to the rich. A 20-rupee tariff on a 90-rupee Chinese teddy bear makes every buyer pay ten rupees more for the local one, a loss each barely notices, while an organised lobby collects the gain. Stigler's axioms explain why this keeps happening: the state has coercive power, whoever steers it benefits, so every private party will rationally try, and concentrated benefits beat diffuse costs. Capital controls show the pattern: the rich hire lawyers to get round them, and everyone else is shut out.
bigIdeas.why: It inverts the usual assumption that intervention protects the weak: when a regulation sounds pious, ask who lobbied for it and who quietly pays. Socialists expect intervention to move wealth from rich to poor; the hosts argue the poor pay most, often by staying poor longer.

bigIdeas.name: Education sorts, it doesn't teach: the Louis Vuitton bag of credentials
bigIdeas.summary: India's education system is optimised for sorting, not teaching: age-sorted classrooms, fixed curricula and high-stakes exams are a 19th-century factory design that rewards only conscientiousness, and coaching shrinks entrance exams to pattern recognition. Universities have become brand factories where students buy a stamp rather than knowledge, and the evidence suggests the brand adds little to what a capable person would have done anyway. Ajay calls a life organised around such status markers the Louis Vuitton bag of credentials, and its greatest victims are the credentialed themselves.
bigIdeas.why: It argues for separating knowledge from credentials, for example by putting every lecture online and hiring for values and ability rather than badges, and it reminds young people and parents that humans blossom in different dimensions at different rates.
